sections.h2: What an HOA painting contractor actually has to deliver
body: Painting one house means pleasing one owner. Painting a community means satisfying a board, an architectural review committee, a management company, and dozens of residents who each want to know when the crew reaches their unit. As an HOA painting contractor in Gainesville, Ocala, and the surrounding counties, we treat that paperwork and communication as part of the job, not an afterthought.

Typical scopes include townhome and villa exteriors, condo buildings, clubhouses and pool houses, entry monuments, mailbox kiosks, perimeter fences, and gatehouses. Many associations bundle in soft washing of roofs, walks, and walls ahead of the repaint so the coating goes onto a clean substrate. Interior common areas, such as hallways, stairwells, and fitness rooms, are scheduled separately so they do not compete with weather-dependent exterior work.

sections.h2: Bid packages your board can compare line by line
body: Boards get stuck when three bids describe three different jobs. Our estimate lists every surface included and excluded, the prep steps, the primer and topcoat by product name, the number of coats, and the working schedule. That makes it possible to put our number next to another company's and see exactly where the difference comes from.

For architectural committees we prepare physical color boards with full-size drawdowns, not tiny chips held up in a meeting room. If your governing documents already lock in an approved palette, we match it from existing paint, a chip, or a leftover can. If the community is refreshing its look, our color consultation service can help the committee narrow body, trim, and accent combinations before the vote.

sections.h2: Phased community repaints and resident communication
body: Most communities are painted in phases, building by building or street by street. Each phase gets a posted schedule and notices so residents know when to move patio furniture, close windows, and park elsewhere. A crew lead is the single point of contact for management, and progress photos give the board real status for its meetings.

We plan exterior phases around Florida weather. October through May is the most forgiving window. In summer, crews start early, track dew point, and watch radar so fresh coatings are not caught by afternoon storms. At the end of each phase we walk the buildings with the manager, note anything that needs attention, and close it out before moving on.

sections.h2: Prep and product choices that stretch the repaint cycle
body: A community repaint is a large capital expense, so the goal is to push the next one as far out as possible. That comes down to prep. Crews wash, scrape back to sound edges, treat mildew, reset nail pops, replace rotted trim and fascia, re-caulk moving joints, and spot-prime bare areas before any finish goes on. Hidden moisture damage behind siding is flagged and priced before it is covered up.

We specify premium Sherwin-Williams and Benjamin Moore lines: 100% acrylic on siding and trim, and elastomeric where stucco shows hairline movement. Two full coats is the baseline. Exterior projects carry a written workmanship warranty of up to 10 years on top of the manufacturer's product warranty, and labelled touch-up paint is left with management for future repairs.

sections.h2: Planning the repaint around reserves and budgets
body: Most associations fund repainting from reserves, and the reserve study rarely lines up neatly with what the buildings actually need. A walkthrough before the budget is finalized helps. The crew lead measures, photographs conditions, and takes moisture readings where something looks wrong, so the board sees which elevations are failing now and which can wait a season.

Because the estimate is broken into lines, the scope can be shaped to fit the money available. Common approaches include painting the sun-beaten south and west elevations first, splitting the community into two budget years, or separating carpentry repairs from the paint contract so they can be approved on their own. A phased community repaint also keeps the job manageable for residents, since only a few buildings are disrupted at once.

Nothing is added to the contract later without written approval. If crews uncover rotted fascia or a failed window seal mid-phase, management gets photos and a written change before any extra work starts, which keeps the board's numbers honest.

We work directly with self-managed HOA boards, community association managers, and property management firms that run rental portfolios. faqs.q: Can you present the bid at our board meeting?
faqs.a: We provide a written, itemized estimate and color boards that are built to be reviewed at a meeting. If the board has questions about scope or products, the crew lead who walked the property can answer them.

faqs.q: Do you provide a certificate of insurance for the association?
faqs.a: Yes. We are licensed, bonded, and fully insured in Florida, and we can issue a certificate of insurance naming your association or management company before work begins.

faqs.q: How are residents kept informed during a phased repaint?
faqs.a: Each phase has a posted schedule and per-building notices, and management has one point of contact on our side. Residents know when to clear patios and close windows before crews arrive.

faqs.q: Can we match our existing approved colors?
faqs.a: Yes. We match from a chip, a painted surface, or a leftover can, and we show full-size drawdowns so the committee can confirm the match before production starts.
